Change and environment

Terrain, flood exposure and checks after storms and floods

Some stretches of a route are steeper, wetter or more exposed than others, and after a cyclone the first question is what has been damaged. We screen your route or site for steep, erosion-prone, drainage-crossing and historically flooded ground before you build or plan maintenance, and after a flood or storm we map the flooded area and check structures and assets along your route, before and after.

Used in: Power & utilities · Rail & roads · Government & public programmes

Request a proposal Open data and credits

What it is

Where the ground works against your asset

Linear assets cross everything: hills, gullies, wetlands and rivers that flood in the rainy season. The stretches where the ground works against you are where erosion undermines towers and pipe cover, where access tracks wash out, and where settlement on low ground is most exposed. In southern Africa, cyclones and floods add another question every few years: what has been damaged along the route, and where should crews go first?

Terrain and flood screening answers the first question before you build or before the rainy season. From elevation data and historical surface-water records we highlight the steep, erosion-prone, drainage-crossing and historically flooded stretches of your route or site, and list the structures and route segments inside them.

Post-event mapping answers the second. After a flood or cyclone, radar shows the flooded area even under cloud, and a reviewer compares imagery captured before and after the event to check structures and assets along your route.

What “historically flooded” means

Seen as water in past satellite records. It is a screening signal for planning and preparedness, not a flood line, a return period or a hydraulic result.

How it works

Before you build, and after an event

Planning and preparedness

Terrain and flood screening

  • Slope and erosion: steep and erosion-prone stretches from elevation data, with drone elevation models for detail where flown.
  • Drainage crossings: where the route crosses concentrated flow paths and river channels.
  • Flood exposure: structures, route segments and sites in historically flooded, low-lying or river-crossing ground.
  • Output: the stretches to look at first, by chainage, in the same register as your structures.

After a cyclone or flood

Post-event mapping

  • Flood extent: from radar imagery captured after the event, which shows larger flooded areas even under cloud.
  • Before and after: a reviewer compares dated optical or drone imagery from before and after the event for structures and assets along your route or site.
  • Output: a map of the flooded area and a list of visible changes to check on the ground, by chainage.
  • Timing: depends on when usable imagery captured after the event exists.

Radar also supports screening between optical surveys in the rainy season, showing larger ground changes, such as clearing and earthworks, even under cloud.

What you receive

Screening your engineers and crews can act on

  • A terrain and water table by route segment or site zone: slope class, erosion-prone ground, drainage crossings and flood exposure
  • Structures and segments in exposed ground, listed from the same register as your encroachment survey
  • After an event: a flooded-area map and a reviewer’s before-and-after list of visible changes, by chainage
  • A PDF report in English or Portuguese and GIS layers in GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile

The services behind it

Every proposal names the services it includes. These are the ones this solution draws on.

Change and repeat surveys

  • All-weather radar change screeningRadar satellite comparisons that show larger ground changes, such as clearing, earthworks and new large buildings, even under rainy-season cloud.

Terrain, water and hazard screening

  • Terrain, slope and erosion screeningSteep, erosion-prone and drainage-crossing stretches of your route or site highlighted from elevation data, with drone elevation models for detail where flown.
  • Flood-exposure screeningStructures, route segments and sites in historically flooded, low-lying or river-crossing areas, highlighted for planning and emergency preparedness.
  • Post-event flood and damage mappingAfter a cyclone or flood, a map of the flooded area and a reviewer's before-and-after check of structures and assets along your route or site.

Elevation screening uses Copernicus DEM data, and flood-exposure screening uses historical surface-water records such as JRC Global Surface Water, each credited as its licence requires.

Limits

What terrain and flood screening is not

What it gives you

  • The stretches of a route or site to look at first for slope, erosion, drainage and flood exposure
  • The flooded area after an event, and visible changes along your route
  • A shared register with your structure survey

What it is not

  • Not a hydraulic model, an official flood line or an insurance rating
  • Not a geotechnical study or engineering design
  • Not a structural assessment or a loss adjustment: visible damage only
  • Not an emergency or early-warning service

Frequently asked questions

Is this a flood model?

No. Flood-exposure screening highlights structures, route segments and sites in areas seen as water in past satellite records, in low-lying ground or at river crossings. It is not a hydraulic flood model, an official flood line or an insurance rating.

How soon after a cyclone can you map the damage?

As soon as usable imagery captured after the event exists. Radar can show the flood extent even under cloud; damage to structures and assets needs optical satellite or drone imagery, which depends on clear weather and, for drones, on permits and safe access. It is not an emergency service.

Is the terrain screening a geotechnical study?

No. It highlights steep, erosion-prone and drainage-crossing stretches from elevation data, so your engineers know where to look. It is not a geotechnical study or engineering design. Drone elevation models add detail where flown.

Can insurers or loss adjusters use the post-event check?

As supporting information: what the imagery shows before and after, on which dates. It covers visible damage only and is not a loss adjustment, a structural assessment or an insurance rating.

Tell us where your route or site meets difficult ground.

Send the route or site, and whether you need screening for planning, preparedness before the rainy season, or a check after an event. We reply with a written proposal.
